solutions.question: Two houses Q and R are 73 metres apart. Using a scale of 1 cm to represent 10 m, construct the locus of a point P which moves such that it is (i) at a distance of 32 metres from Q.
steps: Draw QR = 7.3 cm to represent the 73 m distance between the houses.
Using Q as centre and a radius of 3.2 cm (representing 32 m), draw a circle.
Every point on this circle is 32 m from Q, so the circle is the required locus.
solutions.answer: The locus is a circle centred at Q with radius 3.2 cm.
solutions.figure: A circle with centre Q and radius 3.2 cm, drawn around Q. This is the locus of P.
why: The scale converts the real separation into a drawing length: 73 ÷ 10 = 7.3 cm.
The scale converts 32 m into 3.2 cm, and a circle marks all points that distance from Q.
A circle’s points are all the same radius from its centre, matching the condition.

solutions.question: Two houses Q and R are 73 metres apart. Using a scale of 1 cm to represent 10 m, construct the locus of a point P which moves such that it is (ii) at a distance of 48 metres from the line joining Q and R.
steps: Draw QR = 7.3 cm to represent the 73 m distance between the houses.
At Q and R, construct perpendiculars to QR.
On the perpendiculars, mark points 4.8 cm from QR on the same side of QR, and join these points to draw a line parallel to QR.
Repeat on the other side of QR, marking points 4.8 cm from QR and joining them to draw the second parallel line.
Extend both parallel lines as required. Each is 4.8 cm from QR, so together they form the required locus.
solutions.answer: The locus is the pair of lines parallel to QR and 4.8 cm from QR, one on each side.
solutions.figure: Two lines parallel to QR, each 4.8 cm from QR, one on either side. These lines form the locus of P.
why: The scale converts the real separation into its drawing length.
Perpendiculars provide directions measured at right angles to QR.
The scale converts 48 m to 4.8 cm, and parallel lines keep that distance from QR.
The opposite-side line includes points equally far from QR on the other side.
Both lines contain exactly the points 4.8 cm from QR.

solutions.question: The field is in the form of a rectangle ABCD with mA̅B̅ = 70m and mB̅C̅ = 60 m. Construct the rectangle ABCD using a scale of 1cm to represent 10 m. Show the region inside the field which is less than 30 m from C and farther than 25 m from A̅B̅.
steps: Draw AB = 7 cm to represent 70 m.
At B, construct a perpendicular to AB and mark BC = 6 cm to represent 60 m.
Through C, draw a line parallel to AB; through A, draw a line parallel to BC. Let these lines meet at D to complete rectangle ABCD.
At a distance of 2.5 cm from AB, draw a line parallel to AB inside the rectangle; this represents the line 25 m from AB.
With C as centre and radius 3 cm, draw the arc inside the rectangle; this represents points 30 m from C.
The points inside the rectangle and less than 3 cm from C lie inside this quarter-circle. They are all more than 2.5 cm from AB, since the nearest point of the quarter-circle to AB is 3 cm from AB.
Shade the region inside the quarter-circle and within the rectangle to show the required region.
solutions.answer: The required region is the part of the rectangle inside the quarter-circle centred at C with radius 3 cm.
solutions.figure: Rectangle ABCD measuring 7 cm by 6 cm. Inside it, the required region is the part of the quarter-circle centred at C with radius 3 cm; shade the region inside the arc. Also show the line parallel to AB and 2.5 cm from AB. The shaded region lies farther than 2.5 cm from AB.
why: The scale converts 70 m into 7 cm on the drawing.
A rectangle has right angles, and the scale converts 60 m into 6 cm.
Parallel opposite sides complete a rectangle with the required dimensions.
The scale converts 25 m into 2.5 cm, marking the boundary of the distance condition.
The scale converts 30 m into 3 cm, marking points exactly 30 m from C.
The required points must be inside the 30 m boundary and beyond the 25 m boundary.
Shading highlights the points satisfying both distance conditions inside the field.

definitions.text: Scalene triangle: All sides are of different length.
Isosceles triangles: Two sides are of equal length.
Equilateral triangle: All sides of equal length.
Acute angled triangle: All angles are of measure less than 90⁰.
Obtuse angled triangle: One angle is of measure greater than 90⁰.
Right angled triangle: One angle is of measure equal to 90⁰.
A triangle is a closed figure having three sides and three angles.
The sum of the measure of any two sides of a triangle is always greater than the measure of the third side.
The Ambiguous Case (SSA) occurs when we are given two sides and the angle opposite one of these is less than 90°.

A perpendicular bisector is a line that intersects a line segment at right angle and dividing it into two equal parts. In other words, it intersects the line segment at its midpoint and forms right angles (90°) with it.
A median of a triangle is a line segment that joins a vertex to the midpoint of the side that is opposite to that vertex.

A point of concurrency is the single point where three or more lines, rays or line segments intersect or meet in a geometric figure. This concept is commonly used in triangles, where several important types of points of concurrency exist.
The point of concurrency of perpendicular bisector of the sides of a triangle is called circumcentre.
The point of concurrency of the medians of a triangle is called centroid of the triangle.
An angle bisector of a triangle is a line or ray that divides an angle into two equal parts, creating two smaller angles that are congruent (each having half the measure of the original angle).
The point of concurrency of the angle bisectors of a triangle is called incentre of the triangle.

Altitude is a ray drawn perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side of the triangle. There are three altitudes of the triangle which meet at a single point i.e. the altitudes of a triangle are concurrent.

A locus (plural loci) is a set of points that follow a given rule. In geometry, loci are often used to define the positions of points relative to one another or to other geometric figures. Some common types of loci along with detailed explanations will be discussed.
Equidistant: Let A be a fixed point and B be a set of points. If A is at equal distance from all points of B, then A is said to be equidistant from B.
The locus of a point whose distance is constant from a fixed point is called a circle.

The locus of a point whose distance from a fixed line is constant are parallel lines, ℓ and m e. g. the locus of a point P whose distance is 2.5 cm from a fixed line AB are parallel lines at a distance of 2.5 cm from AB.
The locus of a point whose distance from two fixed points is constant is called a perpendicular bisector.
The locus of a point whose distance is constant from two intersecting lines is called an angle bisector.
If two or more loci intersect at a point P, then P satisfies all given conditions of the loci.

fullMarks: Write the given measurements first, then name the triangle you are constructing.
For a construction, show the compass arcs or angle rays clearly; do not rely only on a finished-looking sketch.
Label every vertex, side length, angle and midpoint used in the construction.
When drawing a perpendicular bisector, show that the arcs from both endpoints intersect above and below the side, then join their intersections.
For concurrency questions, draw all three required lines or rays and mark their common point; state that they are concurrent and name the point (circumcentre, centroid, incentre or orthocentre).
For an altitude, show the right-angle mark where it meets the opposite side or its extension. Extend the side if the perpendicular falls outside the triangle.
For an ambiguous-case question, compare the given side with the perpendicular distance from the vertex to the ray, then state clearly whether zero, one or two triangles are possible.
Use centimetres for construction lengths and degrees for angles, and finish with a sentence identifying the required triangle, locus or centre.
mistakes: Using the wrong two sides or angle when constructing a triangle. Mark the given sides and included or opposite angle before drawing.
Drawing a perpendicular bisector through an endpoint instead of through the midpoint at 90°. Use equal-radius arcs from both endpoints and join the arc intersections.
Confusing a median with a perpendicular bisector. A median joins a vertex to the opposite side’s midpoint; it does not have to meet that side at 90°.
Drawing only one altitude or median when the question asks to verify concurrency. Draw all three and mark their common point.
Calling every triangle centre the same name. Perpendicular bisectors meet at the circumcentre, medians at the centroid, angle bisectors at the incentre and altitudes at the orthocentre.
In an SSA ambiguous case, assuming there is always one triangle. Draw the ray and the arc from the opposite vertex, then count their intersections.
Leaving the final construction unlabeled or not stating the result. Label points and write a concluding sentence naming the triangle, concurrency point or number of possible triangles.

explain.title: Ungrouped and grouped data
explain.body: Data which is not arranged in any systematic order (groups or classes) is called ungrouped data. When the same data is arranged into groups or classes, it is called grouped data.

explain.title: Frequency distribution
explain.body: A distribution or table that represents classes or groups along with their respective class frequencies is called frequency distribution. The frequency tells how many data values fall in each class.

explain.title: Making class intervals
explain.body: First find the range by subtracting the smallest value from the greatest value. Divide the range by the desired number of classes to find the class size, then form the class limits and count the data with tally marks.

explain.title: Unequal class widths
explain.body: When the class widths are unequal, adjust each rectangle height by dividing its class frequency by its class width. These proportional heights are also called adjusted frequencies.

explain.title: Midpoints and frequency polygons
explain.body: A frequency polygon is a line graph of a frequency distribution in which frequencies are plotted against their midpoints. Midpoint is the average value of the lower and upper class limits.

mistakes: Using the range formula in the wrong order: subtract the smallest value from the greatest value.
Starting the class intervals at a value other than the smallest data value when following the textbook method.
Counting a value twice or missing it while making tally marks.
Using the original frequencies as histogram heights when class widths are unequal; divide each frequency by its class width.
Using class limits instead of midpoints for the horizontal values of a frequency polygon.
Forgetting to label axes, state a scale, or join the polygon points with straight lines.

explain.title: What is central tendency?
explain.body: The measure that gives the centre of the data is called measure of central tendency. Therefore, measure of central tendency is used to find out the middle or central value of a data set. It gives one representative value for a whole set of data.

explain.title: Arithmetic mean
explain.body: It is defined as a value of variable which is obtained by dividing the sum of all the values (observations) by their number of observations. For ungrouped data, use x̄ = Σx/n. For grouped data, use x̄ = Σfx/Σf, where x is the midpoint of each class.

explain.title: Median
explain.body: Median is the middle most value in an arranged (ascending or descending order) data set. Median is the value which divides the data into two equal parts i.e., 50% data is before the median and 50% data after it. For grouped data, find cumulative frequencies, locate the n/2-th item and use Median = ℓ + (h/f)(n/2 − c).

explain.title: Mode and weighted mean
explain.body: In a data the values (observation) which appears or occurs most often is called mode of the data. It is the most common value. When observations have different weights, use weighted mean: x̄w = ΣWX/ΣW.

mistakes: Finding a median without arranging ungrouped observations first.
For an even number of values, choosing one middle value instead of averaging the two middle values.
Using class limits instead of class midpoints when finding a grouped arithmetic mean.
For a grouped median, using the wrong cumulative frequency: c is the cumulative frequency before the median class.
For grouped mode, mixing up f1 (the preceding frequency) and f2 (the following frequency).
For weighted mean, dividing by the number of values instead of by the sum of the weights.
Leaving out units or rounding before completing the calculation.

explain.title: Frequency and frequency distributions
explain.body: Frequency is the number of times a value occurs. A frequency distribution organises data into values or classes and records their frequencies.

explain.title: Histograms and frequency polygons
explain.body: A histogram displays frequencies with adjoining rectangles. To make a frequency polygon, plot frequencies at class midpoints and join the points; it can also be drawn on a histogram.

explain.title: Class boundaries and midpoints
explain.body: For integer class limits, class boundaries make neighbouring intervals join. The midpoint, or class mark, is the average of the two class limits.

explain.title: Mean and weighted mean
explain.body: The mean is the sum of observations divided by their number. For a frequency distribution, use Σfx ÷ Σf; for weighted data, the weights determine how much each value contributes.

explain.title: Median, mode and range
explain.body: Arrange data to find the median: choose the middle value, or average the two middle values. The mode occurs most often. The range is the greatest value minus the smallest value.

Forgetting to label graph axes, use an appropriate scale, or plot a frequency polygon at the class midpoints.

definitions.text: Information handling is the process of collecting, organizing, summarizing, analyzing and interpreting numerical data.
So, the collection of meaningful information in the form of facts and numerical figures is known as data.

It can take only some specific values. whole numbers are used to write discrete data. e.g., number of books sold by a shopkeeper, number of patients visited a hospital in a week etc. This data is only obtained by counting.

It can take every possible value in a given interval. Decimal numbers are used to write continuous data. The data is only obtained by measuring e.g., the mass of students in class i.e., 28.5 kg, 26.5 kg, 27.5 kg etc.
Data which is not arranged in any systematic order (groups or classes) is called ungrouped data.
If we arrange the above given data in groups or classes, then it is called grouped data.
Range is the difference between the greatest value and the smallest value i.e., Range = Xₘₐₓ − Xₘᵢₙ
The number of times a value occurs in a data is called the frequency of that value. It is denoted by “f”.

This is a graph of adjacent rectangles constructed on xy plane. A histogram is similar to bar graph but it is constructed for a frequency distribution. In a histogram, the values of the data (classes) are represented along the horizontal axis and the frequencies are shown by bars perpendicular to the horizontal axis. Bars of equal width are used to represent individual classes of frequency table.

A frequency polygon is a closed geometrical figure used to display a frequency distribution graphically. A line graph of a frequency distribution is known as frequency polygon in which frequencies are plotted against their midpoints.
Midpoint is the average value of the lower and upper class limits. Midpoint is also known as class mark.
The measure that gives the centre of the data is called measure of central tendency. Therefore, measure of central tendency is used to find out the middle or central value of a data set.
It is defined as a value of variable which is obtained by dividing the sum of all the values (observations) by their number of observations.

Median is the middle most value in an arranged (ascending or descending order) data set. Median is the value which divides the data into two equal parts i.e., 50% data is before the median and 50% data after it. Median is denoted by X̃.
In a data the values (observation) which appears or occurs most often is called mode of the data. It is the most common value. Mode is denoted by X̂.

Arithmetic Mean is used when all the observations are given equal importance / weight but there are certain situations in which the different observations get different weights. In this situation, weighted mean denoted by X̄_w is preferred.

fullMarks: For a frequency table, show the range and class-size calculation first; then make clear columns for class limits, tally marks, frequency and class boundaries when required.
For a histogram, label both axes, mark class boundaries on the horizontal axis, use a stated scale and draw adjoining rectangles. For unequal class widths, calculate and use adjusted frequencies.
For a frequency polygon, show the midpoint calculation, plot each midpoint against its frequency, join the points with straight lines and extend both ends to the x-axis.
For a grouped mean, include columns for midpoint x and fx (or deviation D and fD); show Σf and Σfx (or ΣfD) before substituting into the formula.
For an ungrouped median, arrange all values in ascending or descending order and state the observation position before giving the answer. For even n, average the two middle observations.
For a grouped median, show the cumulative-frequency column, identify the median class and state ℓ, h, f, n and c before substitution.
For a grouped mode, identify the modal class and clearly state ℓ, h, fₘ, f₁ and f₂. Finish with a sentence giving the answer and its units when the data has units.
mistakes: Using class limits instead of class boundaries on a histogram when the classes are written in inclusive form. Find the boundaries first, such as 24–28 becoming 23.5–28.5.

Finding the median before arranging raw data, or choosing the wrong middle position. Arrange the values first and then use the odd- or even-number formula.
Using the wrong cumulative frequency in the grouped-median formula. Use c as the cumulative frequency before the median class, not the cumulative frequency of that class.
Mixing up the modal-class frequency and its neighbouring frequencies. Use fₘ for the modal class, f₁ for the class before it and f₂ for the class after it.

shortTheory.question: Define frequency distribution.
shortTheory.answer: A distribution or table that represents classes or groups along with their respective class frequencies is called frequency distribution. In other words, the various items of data are classified into certain groups or classes and the number of items lying in each group or class is put against that group or class. The data organised and summarized in this way is known as frequency distribution.

shortTheory.question: Define mode.

explain.title: Use the complement for an opposite event

explain.title: Cards and dice also use outcome counts
explain.body: A standard pack has 52 cards, with 13 cards in each suit. A dice has 6 possible results. Count the results that fit the question, divide by the total, and simplify.

explain.title: Read the event wording carefully
explain.body: “Not” and “neither” ask for outcomes outside the named event. “At least” includes the number stated and any larger numbers in the allowed range.

mistakes: Using the number of favourable outcomes as the total number of outcomes.
Forgetting to include all possible outcomes when dice are thrown as a pair.
Treating “not” or “neither” as the named event instead of its complement.
Miscounting repeated letters in a word, such as counting only one A in MATHEMATICS.
Forgetting to simplify the final fraction.
Reading “at least 20” as only 20 instead of including 20 through 30.

solutions.question:
Let A, B and C are three missiles and they are fired at a target. If the probabilities of hitting the target are P(A) = 1/4, P(B) = 3/7, P(C) = 5/9, respectively.
Find the probabilities of
(i) missile A does not hit the target.
(ii) missile B does not hit the target.
(iii) missile C does not hit the target.
steps: (i) missile A does not hit the target.
Let ‘A′’ be the event that missile A does not hit the target
Thus, the probability of missile ‘A’ does not hit the target is 3/4.
(ii) missile ‘B’ does not hit the target.
Let ‘B′’ be the event missile B does not hit the target
Thus, the probability of missile ‘B’ does not hit the target is 4/7.
(iii) missile ‘C’ does not hit the target.
Let ‘C′’ be the event missile C of not hitting the target
Thus, the probability of missile ‘C’ does not hit the target is 4/9.
why: This begins the first question about a complement.
The given probability is the chance that missile A hits.
Naming the opposite event identifies what we must find.
The complement rule finds the chance that A does not hit.
Subtracting from 1 gives the probability of a miss.
This states the first answer.

Naming the opposite event identifies what we must find.

The given probability is the chance that missile C hits.
Naming the opposite event identifies what we must find.
The complement rule finds the chance that C does not hit.
Subtracting the hit probability from 1 gives the miss probability.
This states the third answer.

solutions.question:
A card is drawn at random, from a pack of 52 playing cards. What is the probability of getting:
(i) a card of heart
(ii) neither spade nor heart
steps: Let ‘A’ be the event of selecting a card of heart.
Thus, the probability of getting a card of heart is 1/4.

[FIGURE: “Total cards = 52” leads to “4 suits”, divided into “13 Spades (Black)”, “13 Clubs (Black)”, “13 Hearts (Red)” and “13 Diamonds (Red)”; each suit contains “1 king”, “1 Queen”, “1 Jack”, “1 Ace” and “(2 – 10) cards”.]
Let ‘B’ be the event of selecting a card of spade or heart
Number of spade and heart cards = 26 ; n(B) = 26
Let ‘B′’ be the event of selecting neither spade nor heart card.
Thus, the probability of getting neither spade nor heart cards is 1/2.
why: This heading separates the first part of the question from the second.
A standard pack has 52 cards, so this is the total number of equally likely choices.
Naming the event makes it easier to write its probability.
Each of the four suits has 13 cards, so hearts have 13 cards.
Probability is favourable outcomes divided by all possible outcomes.
Reducing the fraction gives the simplest form of the probability.
This states the answer for the heart event.
The diagram shows how the 52 cards are divided into four suits of 13 cards each.
This heading separates the second part of the question.
This names the event of drawing a spade or heart, whose opposite is neither suit.
Spades and hearts each have 13 cards, giving 26 cards altogether.
Use the probability rule: favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
Replace the event and total counts with 26 and 52.
This is the simplified probability of drawing a spade or heart.
The complement event contains every card outside the spade-or-heart event.
An event and its complement have probabilities that add to 1.
Substitute the probability of drawing a spade or heart.
Subtracting gives the probability of its complementary event.
This states the required probability for neither suit.

solutions.question: Arshad rolls a dice, with sides labelled L, M, N, O, P, U. What is the probability that the dice lands on consonant?
steps: P (getting a consonant) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of outcomes
why: A die has six labelled faces, so there are six equally likely outcomes.
L, M, N, and P are consonants, giving four favourable faces.
The probability rule compares favourable outcomes with all outcomes.
Substitute four favourable faces and six total faces.
Simplifying the fraction gives the probability in lowest terms.

solutions.question: Shazia throws a pair of fair dice. What will be the probability of getting: sum of dots is at least 4.
steps: The outcomes with sum less than 4 are (1, 1), (1, 2) and (2, 1)
Number of outcomes with sum at least 4 = 36 − 3 = 33
P (sum of dots is at least 4) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of outcomes
P (sum of dots is at least 4) = 33/36
P (sum of dots is at least 4) = 11/12
why: Two dice have six choices each, so the multiplication rule gives 36 ordered outcomes.
Listing sums below 4 identifies exactly the outcomes excluded from the event.
Subtract the excluded outcomes from all outcomes to count sums of at least 4.
The probability rule divides favourable outcomes by all possible outcomes.
Substitute the favourable count and total count.
Simplifying the fraction gives the probability in lowest terms.

solutions.question: Shazia throws a pair of fair dice. What will be the probability of getting: product of both dots is between 5 to 10.
steps: The total number of outcomes when two dice are thrown = 6 × 6 = 36.
The outcomes for which the product of the dots is between 5 and 10 are (1,5), (5,1), (1,6), (6,1), (2,3), (3,2), (2,4), (4,2), (3,3), (2,5), (5,2).
Probability = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of outcomes.
why: Each die has six choices, so the multiplication rule gives 36 ordered outcomes.
Checking the possible pairs identifies every outcome with product from 5 through 10.
Counting the listed pairs gives the number of favourable outcomes.
Use the probability rule to compare favourable outcomes with all outcomes.
Substitute the two counts to obtain the required probability.

solutions.question: Shazia throws a pair of fair dice. What will be the probability of getting: the difference between both the dots is equal to 4.
steps: The outcomes in which the difference between the dots is 4 are (1, 5), (2, 6), (5, 1) and (6, 2)
P (difference between both dots is equal to 4) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of outcomes
P (difference between both dots is equal to 4) = 4/36
P (difference between both dots is equal to 4) = 1/9
why: Two dice each have six choices, so there are 36 ordered outcomes.
Listing pairs with absolute difference 4 finds all favourable outcomes.
Counting those pairs gives the favourable-outcome total.
Use the probability rule: favourable outcomes divided by all outcomes.
Substitute four favourable outcomes and 36 total outcomes.
Simplifying gives the probability in lowest terms.

solutions.question: Shazia throws a pair of fair dice. What will be the probability of getting: number at least 5 on the first dice and the number at least 4 on the second dice.
steps: Outcomes with a number at least 5 on the first dice = 2
Outcomes with a number at least 4 on the second dice = 3
P (number at least 5 on the first dice and at least 4 on the second dice) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of outcomes
P (number at least 5 on the first dice and at least 4 on the second dice) = 6/36
P (number at least 5 on the first dice and at least 4 on the second dice) = 1/6
why: Two dice each have six faces, so the multiplication rule gives 36 outcomes.
Only 5 and 6 meet the first-die condition, giving two choices.
The second die can show 4, 5, or 6, giving three choices.
The choices are independent, so multiply their counts to get favourable pairs.
Use the probability rule to compare favourable pairs with all outcomes.
Substitute six favourable pairs and 36 total outcomes.
Simplify the fraction to give the probability in lowest terms.

solutions.question: One alphabet is selected at random from the word “MATHEMATICS”. Find the probability of getting: vowel.
steps: Total number of alphabets in MATHEMATICS = 11
P (getting a vowel) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of outcomes
why: Counting the letters establishes the total number of equally likely selections.
A, E, and I are the four vowel occurrences in this word.
The probability rule is favourable selections divided by total selections.
Substitute the vowel count and total letter count.

solutions.question: One alphabet is selected at random from the word “MATHEMATICS”. Find the probability of getting: consonant.
steps: Total number of alphabets in MATHEMATICS = 11
P (getting a consonant) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of outcomes
why: Counting the letters establishes the total number of equally likely selections.
Subtracting four vowels from eleven letters leaves seven consonants.
The probability rule is favourable selections divided by total selections.
Substitute the consonant count and total letter count.

solutions.question: One alphabet is selected at random from the word “MATHEMATICS”. Find the probability of getting: an E.
steps: Total number of alphabets in MATHEMATICS = 11
P (getting an E) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of outcomes
why: Counting the letters establishes the total number of equally likely selections.
Checking the word shows that E occurs once.
The probability rule is favourable selections divided by total selections.
Substitute the count of E and the total letter count.

solutions.question: One alphabet is selected at random from the word “MATHEMATICS”. Find the probability of getting: an A.
steps: Total number of alphabets in MATHEMATICS = 11
P(getting A) = Number of A’s / Total number of alphabets
why: Counting the letters establishes the total number of equally likely selections.
Checking the word shows that A occurs twice.
The probability rule compares the number of A's with all letters.
Substitute the count of A and the total letter count.

solutions.question: One alphabet is selected at random from the word “MATHEMATICS”. Find the probability of getting: not M.
steps: Total number of alphabets in MATHEMATICS = 11
Number of alphabets that are not M = 11 − 2 = 9
P(not M) = Number of alphabets that are not M / Total number of alphabets
why: Counting the letters establishes the total number of equally likely selections.
Checking the word shows that M occurs twice.
Subtract the M's from all letters to count selections that are not M.
The probability rule compares favourable selections with all letters.
Substitute the non-M count and total letter count.

solutions.question: One alphabet is selected at random from the word “MATHEMATICS”. Find the probability of getting: not T.
steps: Total number of alphabets in MATHEMATICS = 11
Number of alphabets that are not T = 11 − 2 = 9
P(not T) = Number of alphabets that are not T / Total number of alphabets
why: Counting the letters establishes the total number of equally likely selections.
Checking the word shows that T occurs twice.
Subtract the T's from all letters to count selections that are not T.
The probability rule compares favourable selections with all letters.
Substitute the non-T count and total letter count.

solutions.question: Aslam rolled a dice. What is the probability of getting the numbers 3 or 4? Also find the probability of not getting the numbers 3 or 4.
steps: Total number of outcomes when a dice is rolled = 6
P(getting 3 or 4) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of outcomes
P(not getting 3 or 4) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of outcomes
why: A standard die has six equally likely faces, so there are six possible outcomes.
The event includes exactly the two listed faces, 3 and 4.
Counting the listed faces gives the number of outcomes that meet the event.
Probability is found by dividing favourable outcomes by all equally likely outcomes.
Reducing 2/6 gives the simplest form of the probability.
The remaining four faces form the event's complement.
Counting these remaining faces gives four favourable outcomes.
The same probability rule applies to the complementary event.
Reducing 4/6 gives the simplest form of the probability.

solutions.question: Abdul Hadi labelled cards from 1 to 30 and put them in a box. He selects a card at random. What is the probability that selected card containing: the number 25.
steps: P(getting the card containing 25) = Number of favourable cards / Total number of cards
why: There is one card for each integer from 1 to 30, giving 30 equally likely choices.
Only one card is labelled 25.
Probability equals favourable cards divided by all cards.
The fraction shows one favourable card among 30 equally likely cards.

solutions.question: Abdul Hadi labelled cards from 1 to 30 and put them in a box. He selects a card at random. What is the probability that selected card containing: number between 17 to 22.
steps: P(getting a number between 17 and 22) = Number of favourable cards / Total number of cards
why: The cards numbered 1 through 30 give 30 equally likely choices.
Listing the inclusive range identifies all cards from 17 through 22.
There are six numbers in the listed range.
Probability is favourable cards divided by the total number of cards.
Reducing 6/30 gives the simplest probability.

solutions.question: Abdul Hadi labelled cards from 1 to 30 and put them in a box. He selects a card at random. What is the probability that selected card containing: number at least 20.
steps: P(getting a number at least 20) = Number of favourable cards / Total number of cards
why: The cards numbered 1 through 30 give 30 equally likely choices.
At least 20 includes 20 and every larger card number through 30.
Counting this inclusive list gives 11 favourable cards.
Probability is favourable cards divided by the total number of cards.
The fraction is already in simplest form.

solutions.question: Abdul Hadi labelled cards from 1 to 30 and put them in a box. He selects a card at random. What is the probability that selected card containing: number not 27 and 29.
steps: Numbers that are not 27 and 29 = 28 cards
P(getting a number other than 27 and 29) = Number of favourable cards / Total number of cards
P(getting a number other than 27 and 29) = 28/30 = 14/15
solutions.answer: P(getting a number other than 27 and 29) = 14/15
why: The complete set contains 30 equally likely cards.
Only cards 27 and 29 are excluded, leaving 28 choices.
Subtracting the two excluded cards from 30 counts the favourable cards.
Probability is favourable cards divided by all cards.
Reducing 28/30 gives the simplest form.

solutions.question: Abdul Hadi labelled cards from 1 to 30 and put them in a box. He selects a card at random. What is the probability that selected card containing: number not between 12 to 15.
steps: Number of cards not numbered from 12 to 15 = 30 − 4 = 26
why: There are 30 equally likely cards altogether.
Counting inclusively from 12 through 15 gives four excluded cards.
Subtracting those four cards leaves 26 favourable cards.
Reducing the favourable-to-total fraction gives the probability.

solutions.question: The probability that Ayesha will pass the examination is 0.85. What will be the probability that Ayesha will not pass the examination?
steps: P(Ayesha will not pass) = 1 − P(Ayesha will pass)
why: The stated probability gives the chance of passing directly.
Passing and not passing are complementary outcomes, so their probabilities add to one.
Subtracting the passing chance from one finds the complementary chance.
This subtraction gives the probability of not passing.

solutions.question: Taabish tossed a fair coin and rolled a fair dice once. Find the probability of the following events: tail on coin and at least 4 on dice.
steps: Total outcomes when a coin is tossed and a dice is rolled = 2 × 6 = 12
why: The coin has two outcomes and the die six, so multiplication gives 12 combined outcomes.
These pairs are exactly the outcomes with a tail and a die result of at least four.
Counting the listed pairs gives three favourable outcomes.
The fraction of favourable outcomes simplifies to one quarter.

solutions.question: Taabish tossed a fair coin and rolled a fair dice once. Find the probability of the following events: head on coin and the number 2,3 on dice.
steps: Total outcomes when a coin is tossed and a dice is rolled = 2 × 6 = 12
why: There are two coin outcomes and six die outcomes, giving 12 equally likely pairs.
These pairs match heads with either die result 2 or 3.
There are two favourable pairs in the list.
Reducing 2/12 gives the probability.

solutions.question: Taabish tossed a fair coin and rolled a fair dice once. Find the probability of the following events: head and tail on coin and the number 6 on dice.
steps: Total outcomes when a coin is tossed and a dice is rolled = 2 × 6 = 12
why: Two coin outcomes combined with six die outcomes make 12 equally likely pairs.
Either coin side paired with 6 satisfies the event, giving these two pairs.
Counting those pairs gives two favourable outcomes.
Reducing 2/12 gives the probability.

solutions.question: Taabish tossed a fair coin and rolled a fair dice once. Find the probability of the following events: not tail on coin and the number 5 on dice.
steps: Total outcomes when a coin is tossed and a dice is rolled = 2 × 6 = 12
The only outcome that is tail and 5 is (T, 5)
Number of outcomes that are not tail and 5 = 12 − 1 = 11
why: The coin-and-die experiment has 12 equally likely outcome pairs.
This identifies the single outcome that is both tail and 5.
Subtracting this pair counts outcomes that are not both tail and 5, not outcomes that are not tail and 5.
The requested event is head and 5, so its probability is 1/12, not 11/12.

solutions.question: Taabish tossed a fair coin and rolled a fair dice once. Find the probability of the following events: not head on coin and the number 5 and 2 on dice.
steps: Total outcomes when a coin is tossed and a dice is rolled = 2 × 6 = 12
Outcomes that are head and 5 or 2 = { (H, 5), (H, 2) }
Number of outcomes that are not head and 5 or 2 = 12 − 2 = 10
why: The coin-and-die experiment has 12 equally likely outcome pairs.
These are the head outcomes with die result 5 or 2.
The requested event is tail with 5 or 2, so there are two favourable outcomes, not ten.
Thus the probability is 2/12 = 1/6, not 5/6.

solutions.question: A card is selected at random from a well shuffled pack of 52 plying cards. What will be the probability of selecting: a queen.
steps: Total number of cards in a pack = 52
Number of queens in a pack = 4
why: A standard pack contains 52 cards, so this is the total number of possible outcomes.
Each of the four suits has one queen, giving four favourable cards.
Probability is favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes; simplify the fraction by four.

solutions.question: A card is selected at random from a well shuffled pack of 52 plying cards. What will be the probability of selecting: neither a queen nor a jack.
steps: Number of queens = 4 and number of jacks = 4.
Number of cards that are either a queen or a jack = 4 + 4 = 8.
Number of cards that are neither a queen nor a jack = 52 − 8 = 44.
P(neither a queen nor a jack) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of outcomes.
P(neither a queen nor a jack) = 44/52 = 11/13.
why: All cards in the pack are possible outcomes when one card is selected.
Each of the four suits contains one queen and one jack.
Queens and jacks are separate ranks, so add their counts to find the excluded cards.
Subtract the excluded cards from the pack to count cards meeting the condition.
Probability compares favourable outcomes with all possible outcomes.
Divide 44 by 52 and simplify by four to get the probability.

solutions.question: A card is chosen at random from a pack of 52 playing cards. Find the probability of getting: a jack.
steps: P(getting a jack) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of outcomes.
why: A standard pack has 52 cards, which gives the total possible outcomes.
There is one jack in each of the four suits.
The probability rule uses favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes.
Divide 4 by 52 and simplify to express the probability in lowest terms.

solutions.question: A card is chosen at random from a pack of 52 playing cards. Find the probability of getting: no diamond.
steps: Number of cards that are not diamonds = 52 − 13 = 39.
P(no diamond) = Number of favourable outcomes / Total number of outcomes.
why: A standard pack has 52 cards, giving the total possible outcomes.
Each suit contains 13 cards, so there are 13 diamonds.
Subtract diamonds from the pack to count cards that are not diamonds.
Probability is the number of favourable outcomes divided by all outcomes.
Simplify 39/52 by dividing numerator and denominator by 13.

modules.title: 13.4 Relative Frequency as an Estimate of Probability

bookReference.text: Your textbook, Unit 13, section 13.4, pages 252–253

examTips: A board question may ask you to calculate relative frequencies from a frequency table.
First show the total frequency, N = Σf. Then divide each required event frequency by N.
Write the result as a fraction and, when required, as a decimal. Follow the rounding shown in your textbook.
Marks are earned for finding the correct total, using the correct numerator and denominator, and giving the correct final value.

hints: Find the frequency in the row for X = 3.
Divide that frequency by the total frequency, 43.

Divide 9 by the total frequency, 43.
yourTurn.question: Using the table in Example 8, find the relative frequency for X = 5.

steps.why: The total frequency is the denominator used for every relative frequency.
For each value of X, divide its frequency by the total frequency, 43.
The frequency for X = 3 is 5, so use 5 as the numerator.
The frequency for X = 4 is 6, so use 6 as the numerator.
The frequency for X = 5 is 9, so use 9 as the numerator.
The frequency for X = 6 is 10, so use 10 as the numerator.
The frequency for X = 7 is 8, so use 8 as the numerator.
The frequency for X = 8 is 2, so use 2 as the numerator.

example.question: EXAMPLE 8: Find the relative frequency of the given date. X: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8; f: 3, 5, 6, 9, 10, 8, 2.
example.answer: Σf = 43; relative frequencies for X = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 are 0.07, 0.12, 0.14, 0.21, 0.23, 0.19, 0.04 respectively.

explain.title: Meaning of relative frequency
explain.body: Relative frequency tells us how often a specific event occurs relative to the total number of frequency event or trials. It compares the event’s frequency with the total frequency.

explain.title: The formula
explain.body: Relative frequency = Frequency of specific event / Total frequency = x/N, where N = Σf. Add the frequencies to find N, then divide the event’s frequency by N.

explain.title: Use the frequency table
explain.body: In Example 8, the frequencies add to 43. For X = 6, the frequency is 10, so the relative frequency is 10/43 = 0.23.

mistakes: Using the value of X as the numerator instead of its frequency.
Forgetting to add all frequencies to find the total frequency.
Reversing the division and writing total frequency over event frequency.
Using a different denominator for different values in the same table.
Rounding the decimal differently from the value shown in your textbook.

example.question:
A survey was conducted on 80 students of Grade – IX and asked about their favourite colour. The responses are:

(i) Red colour = 23 students
(ii) Green colour = 15 students
(iii) Pink colour = 25 students
(iv) Blue colour = 10 students
(v) White colour = 7 students.

Find the relative frequency for each colour.

explain.title: Meaning of relative frequency
explain.body: Relative frequency is an estimated probability of an event occurring when an experiment is repeated a fixed number of times.

explain.title: How to calculate it
explain.body: Divide the frequency of the outcome you are interested in by the total frequency. For example, for 23 red responses out of 80 students, calculate 23/80.

explain.title: Reading the result
explain.body: A relative frequency can be written as a fraction, decimal, or percentage. The sum of all the relative frequencies is always equal to or approximately equal to 1.

mistakes: Using the outcome count as the denominator and the total as the numerator.
Using the wrong total when several categories are given.
Writing a percentage without converting the decimal by multiplying by 100.
